transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
A new U.S. Supreme Court term is underway, among the biggest cases on the docket, legal
tests of religious rights and bans on semiautomatic weapons.
This hour, justices are hearing arguments over whether a federal district court has
the power to hear a constitutional challenge on a law that restricts disability benefits
for certain veterans who are incarcerated.
That was preceded by a climate case pitting big oil against local governments, and Piazzina
Totenberg reports.
The opening case before the justices tests whether state and local governments can sue
energy companies for allegedly deceiving the public about the damaging effects of fossil
fuels.
Also on the docket is another Colorado case that centers on a state law that provides
funding for a universal preschool program that's open to all students, regardless of
race, religion, sexual orientation, or gender identity.
A Catholic parish is challenging the program's anti-discrimination provision, contending
that it violates its free exercise of religion.
Nina Totenberg, NPR News, Washington.
Russia is using its jet-powered drones to attack a new target in Ukraine, bridges in
the Ukrainian capital Kyiv.
And Piazz Jovanekakis's reports that drones have hit at least two of six major bridges
over the Niprah River over the last few days.
The Niprah River runs north to south in Ukraine and splits the country in two.
In Kyiv, at least six major bridges across it are essential for transportation.
Cars, buses, trucks, trains, and the metro use these bridges.
Russian drones have repeatedly struck two of them, including one that trolley bus driver
Viktor Krom crosses several times a day.
People have gotten so used to Russian attacks, he says, but life goes on.
You can't just hide from it.
In the last few weeks, Russia's jet-powered drones have been striking Kyiv roughly every
four hours, day or night.
They also struck when German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited the Ukrainian capital on Sunday.
Jovanekakis's NPR News, Kyiv.
One American and two German scientists have been awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology
or Medicine.
NPR's Rob Stein has details.
The Nobel Assembly at the Karolinska Institute in Sweden awarded the prize to two German scientists,
Peter Hegeman and Gerd Nagel, and one American, Karl Deisserhof, at Stanford University.
The three scientists played key roles in discoveries that led to light-controlled switches that
turned nerve cells on and off.
The technique opened a new way to understand the function of neurons known as optogenetics.
The Nobel Committee says the discoveries laid the foundation for a new era of neuroscience,
including helping to understand how the brain forms memories, feelings, and behaviors.
Rob Stein, NPR News.
From Washington, this is NPR.
All of the long-range bombers the U.S. military had stationed at Britain's Fairfield Air Force
Base are now back home.
Vice President J.D. Vance says the decision to withdraw the bombers was made out of an
abundance of caution.
Just over a week ago, British authorities arrested and briefly detained five men near
the base.
The men are now out on bail.
The group is suspected of having links to Iran.
The U.S. has been at war with Iran for more than seven months.
France's Interior Minister says more than 400 schools across the country are blocked
or disrupted today because of massive disruptions students have been protesting overcrowded
classrooms and demanding better learning conditions.
Avengers, Endgame reclaimed the number one spot on Hollywood's all-time worldwide box
office chart over the weekend.
More from NPR's Bob Mondello.
Marvel's superhero epic first became the highest-grossing film in history back in 2019, passing Avatar,
which had held that title for 10 years.
When the original Avatar was re-released in 2022 to promote a sequel and earned enough
to reclaim the top spot, now it's Avengers that has a sequel coming.
So following the same playbook, Endgame has been re-released and has retaken the title.
It's a friendly competition.
Both films are Disney releases and their jockeying reflects rising prices more than attendance.
In terms of tickets sold, neither film comes close to Titanic.
Bob Mondello, NPR News.
You're listening to NPR News.
Want to hear this podcast without sponsor breaks?
Amazon Prime members can listen to NPR News now, sponsor free through Amazon Music.
Or you can also support NPR's vital journalism and get NPR+ at plus.npr.org.
That's plus dot NPR dot org.

topics.text: Supreme Court begins new term with cases on religious rights and semiautomatic weapon bans
Supreme Court hears arguments on federal court power over disability benefits for incarcerated veterans
State and local governments sue energy companies for allegedly deceiving public about fossil fuels
Colorado Catholic parish challenges state universal preschool program's anti-discrimination provision
Russia uses jet-powered drones to attack bridges over Niprah River in Kyiv
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visits Kyiv as Russian drones continue striking city
Two German scientists and one American awarded 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine
Nobel Prize winners credited for discoveries enabling light-controlled nerve cell switches
U.S. military withdraws long-range bombers from Fairfield Air Force Base in Britain
Five men arrested near British air base suspected of links to Iran
More than 400 French schools blocked or disrupted by student protests over overcrowding
Avengers Endgame reclaims number one spot on worldwide box office chart over Avatar
